STEP 1 - Scene: A single whole apple resting on a white square plate, photographed from directly above (top-down view). It is a snack, not a full meal.

STEP 2 - Ruler: The white square plate is roughly 26 cm across its width (a dinner-plate size). Plate area ≈ 26 × 26 × ~0.85 (rounded corners) ≈ 575 cm²; using the apple as a cross-check, the apple's diameter is about 8 cm, which fits a 26 cm plate.

STEP 3 - Items: One red-yellow apple (about 8 cm diameter, whole, with stem cavity visible).

STEP 4 - Area: The apple's top-down footprint is about π × 4² ≈ 50 cm², roughly 9% of the plate's ~575 cm² area.

STEP 5 - Volume: An apple is roughly spherical, so its volume is about 4/3 × π × 4³ ≈ 270 ml (outer envelope, whole fruit).

STEP 6 - Grams: Whole fruit has a bulk density close to water, about 0.85 g/ml for an apple (it is dense, not a loose piece pile). 270 ml × 0.85 ≈ 230 g. A medium apple of this size typically weighs 180–220 g, so I'll take about 200 g.

STEP 7 - Energy: Raw apple ≈ 52 kcal per 100 g. 200 g × 0.52 ≈ 104 kcal.

STEP 8 - Sanity check: One medium apple at about 200 g and roughly 100 kcal is plausible. The plate is mostly empty, which is consistent with a single fruit and not a full meal.
